assumptions._baseWhy: 83,03,27,216 shares in issue at 31-Mar-2026 (Annual Report FY2025-26, capital structure), after the IPO's 3,37,83,782 fresh shares (30-Jun-2025) and 7.67 lakh ESOP shares. Screener's FY26 EPS (₹30.64) implies the same 83.03 cr on net profit of ₹2,544 cr. The company's basic EPS (₹30.97) uses the weighted average (82.14 cr), so our FY26 EPS is ~1% lower than reported.
assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: AUM grew 18.9% in FY25 and 10.7% in FY26 while HDB cut back used/high-value CVs and unsecured business loans; gross loans +11.4% YoY in Q1FY27 (+2.8% QoQ) on disbursements +16%. Management's medium-term aim is nominal GDP + 6-7% (~16-18%) and it is 'very hopeful' of moving toward ~18%, with business loans growing from Q3FY27 and asset finance 'over the next few quarters'. FY27E 14% needs ~3.5% a quarter for Q2-Q4 (festive and March quarters are the strong ones). We reach 16-17% only in FY28-29E, i.e. we do not assume the full 18% arrives. Street: Motilal Oswal ~15% FY27E, Emkay 15.0/17.8/17.9%, JM 14.3/15.6%, Jefferies 15.6/18.3/19%.
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 14.01% FY25, 13.97% FY26, ~14.2% annualised in Q1FY27 (company yield on gross loans 14.19%, seasonally lifted by consumer durables). Management: yields 'fairly constant'; NIM 8%+ is 'non-negotiable'. The mix moves both ways: consumer finance (higher yield) and gold/LAP (lower yield) grow faster than CVs. We hold ~14.0% and trim 5bp a year for competition.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Built in rupees, not as a ratio: (a) lending fees and charges (other financial charges incl. insurance commission, fair-value gains) at 1.22% of average AUM in FY27E (FY26 1.25%, Q1FY27 1.21%), cut by a third of insurance commission (0.13% of AUM) from FY28E for the IRDAI consultation on loan-linked insurance commissions (23-Sep-2026; same treatment as our Cholamandalam report); plus (b) BPO revenue from HDFC Bank of ₹1,260 / 1,300 / 1,340 cr (FY26 ₹1,224 cr, Q1FY27 ₹313 cr; +3% a year, not linked to AUM). Total ₹2,810 / 2,893 / 3,197 cr = 2.212 / 1.979 / 1.877% of average AUM. HDBFS.ctx.js re-checks this build.

bpoBuild._why: Inputs behind feeIncomePct and opexPct (see their notes); not read by the engine. HDBFS.ctx.js checks that feeIncomePct and opexPct equal this build on the model's average AUM.

assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense (Screener) ÷ average borrowings: 7.84% FY25, 7.26% FY26, ~6.96% annualised in Q1FY27 (company cost of borrowings 6.93%, down from 7.57% a year earlier as the 2025 repo cuts reset bank loans, 46% of borrowings). Management: 'range-bound' in Q2; Q3 uncertain. By 30-Sep-2026 most economists expected a 25bp repo hike (Cholamandalam report, market context), so we hold the Q1 level and add 5bp in FY29E. HDB's loans are mostly fixed-rate, so a hike squeezes it until the book reprices.
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Built in rupees: (a) lending opex incl. depreciation at 3.75% / 3.70% / 3.65% of average AUM (FY26 3.78%, Q1FY27 3.81%; management: ~3.7% of gross loans, AI programme 'Shikhar' targets lower servicing and collection costs) plus (b) BPO costs of ₹1,160 / 1,195 / 1,230 cr (BPO revenue less a ₹100 / 105 / 110 cr margin; FY26 margin ₹81 cr, Q1FY27 ₹26 cr), less ₹36 cr a year that Screener moves from other expenses into interest (FY26: Screener interest ₹6,856 cr vs reported finance cost ₹6,820 cr). Total ₹5,888 / 6,568 / 7,412 cr. Lending cost-to-income ~40%, as in Q1FY27 (39.9%).
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Loan losses ÷ average AUM: 2.14% FY25, 2.49% FY26 (stress in CVs and unsecured business loans), 2.32% annualised in Q1FY27 (company basis, flat QoQ despite a seasonally weak quarter). Management: ~2.3% plus/minus as a steady state over three years. FY27E 2.35% leaves room for the monsoon/El Nino risk management flags and a Q2-Q3 that is usually weaker; then 2.3%. Street: Emkay 2.3% FY27-29E; Motilal Oswal 2.3/2.2%; Jefferies 2.4/2.1%.
assumptions._taxRateWhy: Statutory 25.17%; effective 24.9% FY26 (prior-year credits) and 25.6% in Q1FY27.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹4 a share (₹2 interim + ₹2 final) = 13% of EPS; FY25 ₹1 (pre-IPO). Dividend policy adopted 23-Jan-2026 under the RBI's NBFC dividend rules. We keep 13%; a higher payout would lower book growth but not value.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener other income is nil to ₹1 cr in every year; BPO is in fees and opex, not here.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: No equity needed: CRAR 21.29% (Tier 1 17.15%) in Jun-2026 vs a 15% minimum, debt ÷ equity 5.0x. The IPO's ₹2,500 cr fresh issue (Jun-2025) is already in the base. HDFC Bank holds 74.1%, so the 25% public-float rule does not force any sale.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.1 × 6% = 13.1% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.1 as for Bajaj Finance and SBI Cards: AAA funding and an HDFC Bank parent, against a book that is 26% unsecured and 37% vehicle and equipment loans and whose ROE fell to 4.8% in FY21). sustainableRoe 15% = management's 2.5% ROA target × ~6x assets ÷ equity (5.98x at Mar-26), and the median of HDB's FY16-FY26 ROE (15.7%; range 4.8-19.5%). g = 10% long-run book growth (about nominal GDP). Residual income: ROE fades from FY29E to 15% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.3x Mar-28E book, Emkay 2.2x FY28E, Nomura 2.3x Jun-28E, Jefferies 2.5x Jun-28E, Equirus 2.5x FY28E). 2.0x = HDB's own median one-year-forward P/B over the last 12 months (2.28x on all weekly closes, Oct-2025 to Sep-2026) × listed lenders' P/B move against their own 12-month medians on 30-Sep-2026 (−11%, median of ten lenders excluding HDB and Bajaj Housing Finance). The first three months after listing (2.7-3.0x: listing pop, anchor and early lock-in expiries) are left out, as in our Bajaj Housing Finance report; the since-listing median is 2.5x. Bull 2.3x = the 12-month median (sector back to its recent norm); bear 1.6x = justified P/B at a 15% ROE and a 13.1% cost of equity.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (15 − 10) ÷ (13.1 − 10) = 1.61x book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.1% cost of equity, ROE fading to 15%, payout rising to 30%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only, derived the same way: HDB's median one-year-forward P/E over the last 12 months (16.8x on all weekly closes) × listed lenders' P/E move against their 12-month medians (−19.5%) = 13.5x. Bull 17x = the 12-month median; bear 11x = base scaled like the P/B bear (1.6 ÷ 2.0).

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Growth reaches management's ~18% by FY28 as asset finance and business loans turn (AUM +16/18/19%), yields hold 5bp higher and credit cost settles at ~2.15% (FY24 was 1.3%); long-run ROE 17%.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: A weak monsoon and a repo hike hit CV and small-business borrowers: AUM +10/12/13%, credit cost back to ~2.8% (above FY26's 2.5%), funding cost +25bp and yield −10bp; long-run ROE stays at 13%, below the cost of equity.

cover.headline: HDFC Bank's retail lender: an 8% margin, a 2.3% loss rate and a mid-teens ROE, fairly priced at ~2x forward book. We initiate at HOLD.
cover.lead: HDB Financial Services lends ₹1.22 lakh cr to the customers banks find hard to serve: small businesses (38% of loans), truck, equipment and tractor buyers (37%) and consumers buying appliances, cars and two-wheelers (25%), through 1,710 branches and 23.9 mn customers. It also runs a ₹1,224 cr BPO business for its parent, HDFC Bank, which adds only ~2% of profit. The economics are those of a high-yield retail lender: NIM 8.35%, operating costs ~3.8% of loans and loan losses ~2.3% leave an ROA of 2.5% and an ROE of 15% (Q1FY27). The weak spot is growth: loans grew only 11% in FY26 and Q1FY27 while HDB cut back risky products. The street values the stock on **P/B on FY28E book (2.2-2.5x)**. We forecast EPS of ₹39.11 / ₹43.59 / ₹49.50 for FY27-29E and ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}}-{{F.roe.2|pct}}. Applying **2.0x to Sep-28E book of ₹342** (HDB's own 2.28x median over the last 12 months, adjusted for the −11% move in lender multiples) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD.** Our intrinsic checks are lower (justified P/B ₹487, residual income ₹441): at ₹621 the market prices a long-run ROE of ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} against our 15%. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: 23.9 mn customers, an average loan of ~₹1.6 lakh, the top 20 borrowers 0.3% of loans, 74% of the book secured. HDFC Bank's name and a AAA rating keep borrowing costs at ~6.9%, so HDB can lend at 14% yields and still earn an 8%+ margin, which management calls "non-negotiable". Q1FY27 delivered record profit (₹785 cr, +38%) and the lowest Stage 3 in a year (2.34%).

arguments.h: But the returns swing with the credit cycle
arguments.p: Loan losses were 1.3% of loans in FY24, 2.5% in FY26 and 5.1% in Covid (FY21); ROE ranged from 4.8% to 19.5% in six years. Asset finance (37% of loans) still has 3.6% Stage 3; 26% of the book is unsecured. A weak monsoon or a rate hike (both live risks in Sep-2026) hit exactly these borrowers. We model 2.35% loan losses and ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}}-{{F.roe.2|pct}}.

AUM grew 10.7% in FY26 against ~20% at Bajaj Finance and Cholamandalam. Management aims for nominal GDP + 6-7% (~16-18%) and says asset finance and business loans will turn "over the next few quarters". We model 14 / 16 / 17% for FY27-29E: a recovery, but not the full 18%. EPS grows ~17% a year (FY26-29E).

arguments.h: Valuation: 1.9x forward book, down from 3.0x at listing
arguments.p: The stock listed at ₹835 (2.99x next-year book) and trades at ₹621: 2.5x trailing and 1.9x FY28E book, 14.3x FY28E EPS. That is about fair for a 14-15% ROE at our 13.1% cost of equity plus some premium for parentage. Our {{dcf.tp|inr}} is below the street's median ₹804 because our FY28-29E EPS is 6-11% lower: slower growth and a cut to insurance commissions after IRDAI's proposal.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): whether asset finance and business loans start growing, as management said, and whether Stage 3 holds in a seasonally weaker quarter.

RBI's October policy: most economists polled in late September expected a 25bp repo hike; HDB's bank loans (46% of borrowings) reprice up while its vehicle and consumer loans are typically fixed-rate.
IRDAI's final rules on loan-linked insurance commissions (comments due by 25-Oct-2026): ₹455 cr of FY26 income (13% of pre-tax profit) is exposed.
The monsoon and El Nino: management's main monitorable for truck, tractor and rural borrowers in H2FY27.
HDFC Bank's choices: the scope of the BPO contracts and the board-recorded rationale for overlapping products under the RBI's Dec-2025 directions.

sections.title: A retail lender to "aspirational India": small businesses, truckers and consumers, plus a back office for HDFC Bank

blocks.p: HDB Financial Services is a non-deposit-taking NBFC owned 74.1% by HDFC Bank, India's largest private bank. The RBI treats it as an "upper-layer" NBFC, the tier with bank-like rules. It lends to people and small firms with thin credit histories in smaller towns: 71% of its 1,710 branches are in tier-4 towns or smaller, and it reaches customers through 160,000+ dealers and retailers. In FY26 it earned ₹15,788 cr of interest and ₹1,417 cr of lending fees and charges (incl. ₹455 cr of insurance commission), paid ₹6,820 cr of interest, spent ₹4,266 cr running the lending business and set aside ₹2,815 cr for bad loans, leaving ₹3,305 cr of lending profit before tax. The BPO business added ₹81 cr on ₹1,224 cr of revenue.

The arithmetic is "high yield, high cost, high loss". In Q1FY27 the loan book yielded 14.19% and interest cost 5.84% of loans, a net interest margin of 8.35%. Fees add ~1.2%. Running 1,700 branches and 63,500 lending staff costs ~3.8% of loans and bad loans another ~2.32%. What is left is a 2.5% return on assets; ~6x leverage turns that into a 15% ROE. Compare Bajaj Housing Finance: a 9% yield, almost no losses, a similar ROA. HDB earns its return by pricing for risk and then absorbing the losses.

blocks.p: **The BPO business.** About 24,600 of HDB's 88,162 employees (Mar-2026) work for HDFC Bank: sales support (₹737 cr of FY26 revenue), back-office processing (₹207 cr) and collections (₹280 cr). HDFC Bank is the only client and the margin is thin (₹81 cr, 6.6% of revenue, 2.4% of HDB's profit). Revenue halved from ₹2,634 cr in FY23 to ₹1,217 cr in FY25 and has been flat since. In our model BPO revenue sits in fees and its costs in operating expenses, as on Screener, and both are forecast in rupees, so BPO adds ~₹100-110 cr a year and does not grow with the loan book.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** HDB is three lenders with different cycles under one roof. Enterprise lending (mostly loans against property) is steady and secured; asset finance (trucks, equipment, tractors) moves with freight, monsoons and infrastructure spending and is where losses come from (Stage 3 3.6%); consumer finance (durables, cars, two-wheelers, personal loans) is short-dated, fast-growing and partly unsecured. Diversification smooths the cycle; it does not remove it.

sections.title: Nineteen years, two credit cycles and an IPO the RBI required

blocks.p: HDFC Bank set HDB up in 2007 (registered in Ahmedabad) to lend where the bank did not: smaller tickets, thinner files, smaller towns. It grew AUM from ₹25,906 cr in FY16 to ₹1,18,733 cr in FY26 (16% a year) mostly on its own capital and retained profit. Two credit cycles shaped it: the IL&FS-to-Covid shock (FY20-FY22: gross NPA up to 5.0%, ROE down to 4.8%, AUM flat for three years) and the FY25-FY26 stress in trucks and unsecured business loans (credit cost back to 2.5%). The listing was not optional: the RBI's scale-based rules require upper-layer NBFCs to list within three years of being identified, and HDB was on the first list in 2022. The ₹12,500 cr IPO (Jun-2025) was mostly HDFC Bank selling (₹10,000 cr); HDB raised ₹2,500 cr.

sections.title: Retail NBFCs: a big, under-served market, a credit cycle just ending, and banks competing for the best customers

blocks.p: HDB's customers (small shopkeepers and manufacturers, owner-drivers and small fleet operators, first-time borrowers buying a phone or a two-wheeler) are the part of India that banks under-serve. That is a large and growing market, and NBFCs have taken share in it for a decade. FY25-FY26 brought a credit cycle: unsecured business loans and microfinance went bad across the industry, and used and small-fleet truck loans followed. HDB cut back, which is why it grew only ~11% in FY26. By Q1FY27 managements across the sector were describing the stress as "over"; HDB's CFO said "we are completely over it as at the March quarter" (Q4FY26 call).

Competition is product by product. In trucks and equipment HDB faces Shriram Finance, Cholamandalam and the banks; in tractors Mahindra Finance; in consumer durables Bajaj Finance; in two-wheelers and cars the captive and bank lenders; in loans against property everyone. Its parent, HDFC Bank, competes with it in car, two-wheeler, personal and business loans. HDB's edge is reach into small towns and customers without credit files, not price.

sections.title: Growth: 11% for two years while HDB cleaned up; consumer loans and gold are growing, trucks and business loans are not

blocks.p: Gross loans grew 11.4% in the year to Jun-2026 (₹1,09,342 cr → ₹1,21,846 cr) and 2.8% in the quarter. The split is stark. Consumer finance grew +21%, led by consumer durables (+51%) and car loans (+21%); gold loans doubled from a small base. Asset finance grew +9% after HDB walked away from high-value, low-return truck products, and unsecured business loans shrank 8% as HDB tightened after the FY25 stress. Management says the cleanup is done: "a large part of that work has been done… you should start to see growth coming through" (CFO, Q1FY27 call), with business loans growing again from Q3FY27.

sections.title: Three verticals: steady mortgages, cyclical trucks, fast but short-dated consumer loans

blocks.p: **Enterprise lending (₹45,742 cr, 38%).** Mostly loans against property (₹26,422 cr; average ticket ₹47 lakh, ~10-year tenor) and secured business loans, plus ₹11,497 cr of unsecured business loans (₹3 lakh tickets), salaried personal loans and a young gold-loan book (₹1,874 cr, offered in ~500 branches). Mortgages are the steady part: LAP grew 13% and Stage 3 in the vertical is 1.6%. Unsecured business loans were the problem in FY25-FY26 and are only now being grown again.

**Asset finance (₹45,009 cr, 37%).** Loans for commercial vehicles (₹29,503 cr, new and used), construction equipment (₹12,444 cr) and tractors (₹3,062 cr), mainly to owner-drivers, small fleets and contractors; HDB says it has little exposure to large fleets on fixed contracts. This is where losses concentrate: Stage 3 rose from 3.1% (Mar-25) to 4.3% (Dec-25) and is back to 3.6%. HDB has refocused on used vehicles and dropped high-value, low-return products; volumes in the products it wants are at records (May-2026), but the book grew only +9%.

**Consumer finance (₹31,095 cr, 25%).** Consumer-durable loans (₹6,759 cr; average ₹18,000, ~1 year), car loans (₹10,584 cr), two-wheelers (₹3,747 cr), relationship personal loans to existing customers (₹9,448 cr) and a small microfinance pilot (₹558 cr). It grew +21% and has the best asset quality (Stage 3 1.6%, cover 70%), helped by short tenors and high provisioning. It is also the main source of new customers (23.9 mn, +19%), whom HDB then cross-sells.

blocks.callout: **So what:** the mix is drifting toward consumer loans (25.5% of the book from 23.5% a year ago), which lifts yields and fees but shortens the book and raises the unsecured share. If asset finance does not turn, HDB grows ~12-13% with a richer but riskier mix; if it does, 16-18% is reachable. Our base case sits between.

sections.title: NIM: up to 8.35% as funding got cheaper; management's floor is 8%, and a rate hike is the threat

blocks.p: HDB's reported NIM (net interest income ÷ average gross loans) rose from 7.55% in Q4FY25 to 8.35% in Q1FY27. Yields barely moved (13.9-14.2%); the gain came from funding: the RBI's 2025 rate cuts reached bank loans (46% of borrowings), and the cost of borrowings fell from 7.57% to 6.93% in a year. Management's line: NIM of "8%+ is a non-negotiable" (Q4FY26 call); yields have been held and the mix (more consumer loans) helps. The risk runs the other way now. Vehicle and consumer instalment loans, most of HDB's book, are typically fixed-rate, so when rates rise its funding cost moves first; by late September 2026 most economists expected a 25bp hike.

blocks.p: **Why losses are structurally ~2-2.5%:** HDB lends to borrowers with thin files and volatile incomes (owner-drivers, small traders, first-time borrowers), much of it unsecured (26%) or against depreciating vehicles. In good years (FY24) losses fall to ~1.3%; in bad ones (FY21) they reach 5%. Provisions held (₹3,915 cr in Jun-2026, 3.2% of loans) and a 56% cover on Stage 3 are adequate for a normal year, not for a Covid. The ECL model is refreshed every quarter on product-level loss histories; management says there are no one-off overlays.

Each 10bp is ~3.0% of FY28E profit. The bear case adds 50bp (back above FY26's 2.5%); a Covid-style 4-5% year would wipe out most of a year's profit, which is why we use a 1.1 beta.

sections.title: Funding: AAA, diversified and in surplus in every maturity bucket up to five years

blocks.p: HDB borrows like a top-rated corporate. In Jun-2026 its ₹1.02 lakh cr of borrowings were 45.5% bank term and working-capital loans, 29.4% bonds (NCDs), 12.3% foreign-currency loans (ECBs, hedged), 5.3% subordinated debt, 4.1% securitisation, 1.9% commercial paper and 1.5% perpetual debt. HDFC Bank itself lent ₹8,767 cr (Mar-2026), ~9% of borrowings. Long-term debt is rated AAA by CRISIL and CARE. Assets mature ahead of liabilities: the cumulative gap is positive in every bucket up to five years, and the liquidity coverage ratio was 159% in Q1FY27 (daily average). The cost of borrowings was 6.93% in Q1FY27, down from 7.57% a year earlier. The CFO keeps commercial paper under 2% as "dry powder".

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** NBFCs fail on funding before they fail on credit. HDB's funding is as good as a non-bank's gets, and the HDFC Bank name is a real cost advantage over stand-alone lenders to the same customers. It is still not a bank: it cannot take deposits, and 46% of its borrowings reprice with bank lending rates.

sections.title: Capital: 21% CRAR after the IPO; ROE rises only if leverage does

blocks.p: Capital adequacy was 21.29% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 17.15%) against a 15% minimum; debt was 5x equity. The IPO added ₹2,500 cr in Jun-2025, which is one reason ROE fell to 13.9% in FY26. HDB pays out ~13% of profit as dividends (₹4 a share for FY26) and keeps the rest. With equity growing ~13-14% a year and AUM 14-17%, leverage rises only slowly and CRAR stays above 19% on our rough proxy: no new equity is needed in our forecast, and any equity from HDFC Bank would now need RBI approval under the Dec-2025 directions.

sections.title: Profit has doubled since FY22, but ROE peaked at 19.5% in FY24 and the IPO reset it to ~14-15%

blocks.p: HDB's net profit went from ₹1,011 cr in FY22 to ₹2,544 cr in FY26, and its AUM from ₹61,444 cr to ₹1,18,733 cr (18% a year). The path was not smooth. FY21-FY22 were Covid years (loan losses of 5.1% and 4.0% of loans, ROE 4.8% and 11.2%). FY23-FY24 were the best years in its history: loan losses fell to 1.3-2.0% and ROE reached 19.5%. Then stress in commercial vehicles and unsecured business loans pushed loan losses back to 2.1% (FY25) and 2.5% (FY26); profit fell 12% in FY25 and recovered 17% in FY26. ROE fell to 13.9% in FY26 because of those losses and because the IPO added ₹2,500 cr of equity in Jun-2025. Q1FY27 was the best quarter yet (PAT ₹785 cr, ROE 15.0%).

sections.title: HDFC Bank: a parent that lends its name and funding, sits in the same markets, and is bound by bank-group rules

blocks.p: HDFC Bank owns 74.12% of HDB (about 61.5 cr shares). Unlike Bajaj Finance at Bajaj Housing Finance, it does not have to sell: the public already holds 25.9%, above the 25% minimum. The investor lock-ins have expired (the last big one on 2-Jan-2026, 48 cr shares); HDFC Bank's own minimum-contribution lock-in normally runs 18 months from the IPO (we could not confirm its date), and it has said nothing about selling more. So the overhang question is not supply; it is what HDFC Bank wants HDB to be.

blocks.p: **The regulation that nearly changed everything.** In Oct-2024 the RBI proposed that only one entity in a bank group could run a given business and that there be "no overlap" in lending between a bank and its group companies. HDFC Bank and HDB overlap in car, two-wheeler, personal and business loans, so the draft raised the prospect of HDB being merged, shrunk or reshaped, and it hung over the IPO. On 1-Oct-2025 the Governor said the restriction was being removed; the final directions (28-Nov and 5-Dec-2025) keep "one entity per business" only "as a principle" and allow overlap where the bank's board records a rationale such as segmentation. What remains: HDB is treated as an upper-layer NBFC and must follow bank-style limits on certain loans (against the parent's shares, to its directors, for land, IPO and ESOP funding), and HDFC Bank needs RBI approval to put more equity in. None of these touch HDB's core products.

**The BPO business: small, shrinking and dependent.** BPO revenue halved between FY23 and FY25 (₹2,634 cr → ₹1,217 cr) and has been flat since; profit is ₹81 cr. The annual reports do not say why it shrank. It employs roughly a quarter of HDB's staff for ~2% of its profit. If HDFC Bank took the work in-house, HDB would lose ~₹0.7 of EPS (~2%): a nuisance, not a thesis. We forecast BPO revenue +3% a year and a ₹100-110 cr margin, explicitly and separately from lending.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** on balance the parent is a clear positive: it gives HDB a funding cost and a brand no stand-alone lender to these customers has. The costs are subtler. HDFC Bank decides which customers and products it keeps for itself, HDB's growth plans have to fit the group's, and the minority shareholder has no say in either. We see no sign that HDFC Bank wants to sell or shrink HDB, and the regulatory risk that dominated the IPO is gone. We do not put a holding-company or "parent" discount on the stock; we do not put a premium on it either.

sections.title: Q1FY27: record profit, Stage 3 down, margin up; growth still ~11%

blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) was HDB's most profitable quarter: PAT ₹785 cr (+38.3%), ROA 2.5%, ROE 15.0%. Net interest income grew 19.9% on loans up only 11.4%, because the margin widened (NIM 8.35% vs 7.74% a year earlier) as funding costs fell. Lending costs grew 11%, slower than income, so cost-to-income fell to 39.9% (42.7%). Loan losses were flat at ₹697 cr and Stage 3 fell to 2.34% in what is usually a weak quarter. The one soft number was growth: disbursements +16.2% YoY but −11.5% QoQ, asset finance and business loans still flat. Management does not give annual guidance; its standing aims are below.

blocks.p: **What FY27E needs.** Our FY27E profit of ₹{{F.pat.0|num}} cr (+{{F.patGrowth.0|pct}}) needs ~₹821 cr a quarter for Q2-Q4 against ₹785 cr in Q1, +5% above Q1, as the book grows ~3.5% a quarter and margins hold. Two things could break it: a repo hike (funding first, loans later) and a monsoon-driven rise in truck and tractor delinquencies in H2. Motilal Oswal (₹3,310 cr) is a little above us, Emkay (₹3,182 cr) a little below.

blocks.callout: **Our read:** management has delivered what it controls (margin, costs, the asset-quality cleanup) and is behind on what depends on demand and risk appetite (growth). Its words on growth have been hopeful rather than firm ("let us deliver on our numbers and we'll discuss in a few months"). We model the margin and loss rate it guides to and a growth recovery below its aim.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audits and simple products; watch insurance fees and the related-party BPO line

blocks.p: We rate accounting **GREEN**. The joint statutory auditors (Kalyaniwalla & Mistry LLP and G.D. Apte & Co.) gave an unmodified opinion on FY26; the key audit matters were the expected-credit-loss provision and IT systems, as at every lender. Products are plain instalment loans; there is almost no off-balance-sheet lending (AUM is 0.2% above gross loans); provisions are recalculated every quarter on product-level loss histories, and management says there are no one-off overlays. Points to watch:

bullets: **Insurance commission:** ₹455 cr in FY26, up 64% from ₹277 cr, about 13% of pre-tax profit. It is the fastest-growing fee line and the one IRDAI's Sep-2026 proposal targets. We cut a third of it from FY28E.

**BPO revenue is 100% related-party:** ₹1,224 cr billed to HDFC Bank (sales support ₹737 cr, back office ₹207 cr, collections ₹280 cr). Approved by shareholders and the audit committee; pricing is not disclosed. Profit is small (₹81 cr).

**One-offs:** the new labour codes cost ₹61 cr in FY26 (₹56 cr lending, ₹5 cr BPO); FY26 PAT would have been ₹2,586 cr without it. Tax credits for earlier years (₹27 cr in FY26, ₹60 cr in FY25) flattered the tax rate.

**Screener vs company:** Screener moves ~₹35 cr a year from other expenses into interest, and its quarterly gross-NPA row runs one quarter behind the company's Stage 3; we use company figures for asset quality. Screener's FY26 EPS (₹30.64) uses year-end shares; the company's basic EPS is ₹30.97.

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 HDB had ₹1,23,651 cr of assets: ₹1,14,690 cr of loans (net of provisions), ₹3,748 cr of investments and ₹1,673 cr of cash (its liquidity buffer), ₹1,337 cr of derivative assets (hedges on foreign-currency borrowings) and ₹773 cr of fixed assets. sections.title: Our honest summary: a good lender at a fair price, waiting for growth

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a diversified retail lender with HDFC Bank's name and AAA funding, 23.9 mn customers in small-town India, an 8%+ margin, a cleaned-up book (Stage 3 2.34%) and record profit (ROA 2.5%, ROE 15.0% in Q1FY27). **What you are paying:** 2.5x trailing book, 1.9x our FY28E book and 14.3x FY28E EPS for an ROE of ~14.4% against a 13.1% cost of equity. assumptions._note: HDB Financial Services (standalone = the whole company; no subsidiaries) lender model, as of 30-Sep-2026 on a Q1FY27 basis. Sources: Q1FY27 presentation (15-Jul-2026) and call transcript (filed 20-Jul-2026); Q4FY26 presentation and call (15-Apr-2026); Annual Report FY2025-26; Screener.in standalone statements. The BPO business (services to HDFC Bank) is kept inside the lender layout explicitly: its revenue sits in fees & other income and its costs in operating expenses, exactly as Screener reports them, and both are forecast in rupees (see _feeIncomePctWhy and _opexPctWhy), so the Screener tie-out is exact and BPO does not grow with AUM.

history._why: Closing AUM and lending loan losses (impairment on financial instruments, all lending) from the company's 11-year snapshot (Q1FY27 presentation p32), which ties to the audited P&L. Fees & other income = revenue from operations − interest income (audited P&L: BPO sale of services + other financial charges incl. insurance commission + fair-value gains). Screener revenue − these fees = reported interest income within ₹6 cr in every year. FY21 fee split not on file (FY2021-22 annual report not found).

src.all: Q1FY27 presentation p32 (11-year snapshot); Annual Reports FY2022-23, FY2023-24 and FY2025-26 (statement of profit and loss)

assumptions._baseWhy: 83,03,27,216 shares in issue at 31-Mar-2026 (Annual Report FY2025-26, capital structure), after the IPO's 3,37,83,782 fresh shares (30-Jun-2025) and 7.67 lakh ESOP shares. Screener's FY26 EPS (₹30.64) implies the same 83.03 cr on net profit of ₹2,544 cr. The company's basic EPS (₹30.97) uses the weighted average (82.14 cr), so our FY26 EPS is ~1% lower than reported.
assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: AUM grew 18.9% in FY25 and 10.7% in FY26 while HDB cut back used/high-value CVs and unsecured business loans; gross loans +11.4% YoY in Q1FY27 (+2.8% QoQ) on disbursements +16%. Management's medium-term aim is nominal GDP + 6-7% (~16-18%) and it is 'very hopeful' of moving toward ~18%, with business loans growing from Q3FY27 and asset finance 'over the next few quarters'. FY27E 14% needs ~3.5% a quarter for Q2-Q4 (festive and March quarters are the strong ones). We reach 16-17% only in FY28-29E, i.e. we do not assume the full 18% arrives. Street: Motilal Oswal ~15% FY27E, Emkay 15.0/17.8/17.9%, JM 14.3/15.6%, Jefferies 15.6/18.3/19%.
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 14.01% FY25, 13.97% FY26, ~14.2% annualised in Q1FY27 (company yield on gross loans 14.19%, seasonally lifted by consumer durables). Management: yields 'fairly constant'; NIM 8%+ is 'non-negotiable'. The mix moves both ways: consumer finance (higher yield) and gold/LAP (lower yield) grow faster than CVs. We hold ~14.0% and trim 5bp a year for competition.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Built in rupees, not as a ratio: (a) lending fees and charges (other financial charges incl. insurance commission, fair-value gains) at 1.22% of average AUM in FY27E (FY26 1.25%, Q1FY27 1.21%), cut by a third of insurance commission (0.13% of AUM) from FY28E for the IRDAI consultation on loan-linked insurance commissions (23-Sep-2026; same treatment as our Cholamandalam report); plus (b) BPO revenue from HDFC Bank of ₹1,260 / 1,300 / 1,340 cr (FY26 ₹1,224 cr, Q1FY27 ₹313 cr; +3% a year, not linked to AUM). Total ₹2,810 / 2,893 / 3,197 cr = 2.212 / 1.979 / 1.877% of average AUM. HDBFS.ctx.js re-checks this build.

bpoBuild._why: Inputs behind feeIncomePct and opexPct (see their notes); not read by the engine. HDBFS.ctx.js checks that feeIncomePct and opexPct equal this build on the model's average AUM.

assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense (Screener) ÷ average borrowings: 7.84% FY25, 7.26% FY26, ~6.96% annualised in Q1FY27 (company cost of borrowings 6.93%, down from 7.57% a year earlier as the 2025 repo cuts reset bank loans, 46% of borrowings). Management: 'range-bound' in Q2; Q3 uncertain. By 30-Sep-2026 most economists expected a 25bp repo hike (Cholamandalam report, market context), so we hold the Q1 level and add 5bp in FY29E. HDB's loans are mostly fixed-rate, so a hike squeezes it until the book reprices.
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Built in rupees: (a) lending opex incl. depreciation at 3.75% / 3.70% / 3.65% of average AUM (FY26 3.78%, Q1FY27 3.81%; management: ~3.7% of gross loans, AI programme 'Shikhar' targets lower servicing and collection costs) plus (b) BPO costs of ₹1,160 / 1,195 / 1,230 cr (BPO revenue less a ₹100 / 105 / 110 cr margin; FY26 margin ₹81 cr, Q1FY27 ₹26 cr), less ₹36 cr a year that Screener moves from other expenses into interest (FY26: Screener interest ₹6,856 cr vs reported finance cost ₹6,820 cr). Total ₹5,888 / 6,568 / 7,412 cr. Lending cost-to-income ~40%, as in Q1FY27 (39.9%).
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Loan losses ÷ average AUM: 2.14% FY25, 2.49% FY26 (stress in CVs and unsecured business loans), 2.32% annualised in Q1FY27 (company basis, flat QoQ despite a seasonally weak quarter). Management: ~2.3% plus/minus as a steady state over three years. FY27E 2.35% leaves room for the monsoon/El Nino risk management flags and a Q2-Q3 that is usually weaker; then 2.3%. Street: Emkay 2.3% FY27-29E; Motilal Oswal 2.3/2.2%; Jefferies 2.4/2.1%.
assumptions._taxRateWhy: Statutory 25.17%; effective 24.9% FY26 (prior-year credits) and 25.6% in Q1FY27.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹4 a share (₹2 interim + ₹2 final) = 13% of EPS; FY25 ₹1 (pre-IPO). Dividend policy adopted 23-Jan-2026 under the RBI's NBFC dividend rules. We keep 13%; a higher payout would lower book growth but not value.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener other income is nil to ₹1 cr in every year; BPO is in fees and opex, not here.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: No equity needed: CRAR 21.29% (Tier 1 17.15%) in Jun-2026 vs a 15% minimum, debt ÷ equity 5.0x. The IPO's ₹2,500 cr fresh issue (Jun-2025) is already in the base. HDFC Bank holds 74.1%, so the 25% public-float rule does not force any sale.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.1 × 6% = 13.1% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.1 as for Bajaj Finance and SBI Cards: AAA funding and an HDFC Bank parent, against a book that is 26% unsecured and 37% vehicle and equipment loans and whose ROE fell to 4.8% in FY21). sustainableRoe 15% = management's 2.5% ROA target × ~6x assets ÷ equity (5.98x at Mar-26), and the median of HDB's FY16-FY26 ROE (15.7%; range 4.8-19.5%). g = 10% long-run book growth (about nominal GDP). Residual income: ROE fades from FY29E to 15% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.3x Mar-28E book, Emkay 2.2x FY28E, Nomura 2.3x Jun-28E, Jefferies 2.5x Jun-28E, Equirus 2.5x FY28E). 2.0x = HDB's own median one-year-forward P/B over the last 12 months (2.28x on all weekly closes, Oct-2025 to Sep-2026) × listed lenders' P/B move against their own 12-month medians on 30-Sep-2026 (−11%, median of ten lenders excluding HDB and Bajaj Housing Finance). The first three months after listing (2.7-3.0x: listing pop, anchor and early lock-in expiries) are left out, as in our Bajaj Housing Finance report; the since-listing median is 2.5x. Bull 2.3x = the 12-month median (sector back to its recent norm); bear 1.6x = justified P/B at a 15% ROE and a 13.1% cost of equity.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (15 − 10) ÷ (13.1 − 10) = 1.61x book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.1% cost of equity, ROE fading to 15%, payout rising to 30%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only, derived the same way: HDB's median one-year-forward P/E over the last 12 months (16.8x on all weekly closes) × listed lenders' P/E move against their 12-month medians (−19.5%) = 13.5x. Bull 17x = the 12-month median; bear 11x = base scaled like the P/B bear (1.6 ÷ 2.0).
